content: Eosin is a fluorescent acidic compound that carries a negative charge. It binds to and forms salts with basic (positively charged) compounds, such as proteins that are positively charged due to the presence of amino acid residues like arginine and lysine. When eosin interacts with these basic substances, it stains them a dark red or pink color. This staining effect is a result of the chemical action of bromine on fluorescein. Eosin is not only used to stain proteins in the cytoplasm but is also effective in staining collagen and muscle fibers, making these structures visible under a microscope. Structures that readily take up eosin staining are referred to as eosinophilic. The term eosin is derived from the Ancient Greek word Eos, which means dawn, and is also the name of the Greek goddess of the dawn. There are two closely related chemical compounds commonly referred to as eosin. The most frequently used variant is Eosin Y, also known by several other names, including eosin Y ws, eosin yellowish, Acid Red 87, C.I. 45380, bromoeosine, bromofluoresceic acid, and D&C Red No. 22. Eosin Y has a slightly yellowish hue. The other variant is Eosin B, which is also known as eosin bluish, Acid Red 91, C.I. 45400, Saffrosine, Eosin Scarlet, or imperial red. Eosin B has a faint bluish tint. These two dyes are chemically similar and can be used interchangeably. The choice between Eosin Y and Eosin B typically depends on personal preference or traditional practices. Chemically, Eosin Y is a tetrabromo derivative of fluorescein, while Eosin B is a dibromo dinitro derivative of fluorescein. In histology, eosin is most commonly used as a counterstain in combination with hematoxylin in the hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining technique. H&E staining is one of the most widely used methods in histological studies. When tissues are stained with hematoxylin and eosin, the cytoplasm appears pink to orange, while the nuclei are stained dark blue or purple. Eosin also stains red blood cells a bright red color. Typically, Eosin Y is used for staining at concentrations ranging from 1% to 5% weight by volume, dissolved in either water or ethanol. To prevent mold growth in aqueous eosin solutions, thymol is sometimes added. Additionally, a small amount of acetic acid (0.5%) is often included to produce a deeper red stain in tissues. It is important to note that eosin is classified as a Group 3 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).
